findings.title: Unverified remote script piped into sh at build time (supply-chain RCE)
findings.whyItBreaks: The build executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh returns, with zero integrity verification: no checksum pinning, no signature. With -sL, curl silently follows redirects, so a DNS rebind, domain repoint, or redirect can substitute arbitrary code that runs with full privileges during image build (and in CI, with CI's network access, cache, and any mounted secrets). Anyone who controls or compromises that endpoint controls every image built from this Dockerfile.

findings.title: Failed download is swallowed: curl|sh pipeline hides install errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Pipeline exit status is the LAST command's, so `RUN curl -sL <url> | sh` returns sh's status, not curl's. On a network-level failure (DNS, refused, TLS) curl exits non-zero but sh receives empty stdin and exits 0 -> the RUN step succeeds and the image is built without whatever the script installs; the loss only surfaces later at runtime. Additionally, without `-f`, curl exits 0 on HTTP error statuses (404/5xx) and pipes the error-page body into sh, producing garbage execution or a misleading syntax error instead of a download failure. Either way the build's success/failure signal is wrong.

findings.title: Remove unverified `curl | sh` remote-code-execution build step
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN pipes a network-fetched script straight into sh with no pinned version, checksum, or signature: whatever the host serves at build time executes with full build privileges and its effects ship inside the image (before COPY/CMD at lines 4-5), so any compromise of the host or the path to it becomes artifact compromise. `example.com` is an IANA-reserved placeholder (RFC 2606) that serves a static HTML page, so the step cannot even legitimately install anything — it pipes markup into sh. Additionally the pipeline swallows curl's failure signal: Docker RUN only inspects the final command's exit status, so a failed/empty download makes sh exit 0 and the build silently succeeds without the intended tool (`-s` also suppresses curl's error output), leaving a half-built image indistinguishable from a good one.

findings.title: Unverified remote script piped to shell at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the remote host returns as code during image build, with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no control over the artifact source (example.com is an IANA-reserved documentation domain, not a controlled artifact origin). Any compromise or hijack of that host/network path yields arbitrary code execution inside the build (with access to build context and any secrets passed at build time) that is then baked into the published image. This is the canonical supply-chain anti-pattern; a strict reviewer blocks merge on it.

findings.title: curl failure silently swallowed: -s without -f, pipeline exits with sh's status
findings.whyItBreaks: Two added mechanisms discard the failure signal. (1) `curl -sL` lacks `-f/--fail`: an HTTP error response (example.com serves no /install.sh, so a 404 body is the expected response) is written to stdout and piped into `sh` for execution; (2) the pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s, not curl's — on a network-level curl failure the shell receives empty input and exits 0. Either way the RUN step can exit 0, so `docker build` — which gates success solely on RUN's exit status — records the image as correctly built while the tool was never installed (or an error page was interpreted as shell). The build/publish pipeline cannot distinguish failed install from success. This is TRIGGER D: swallow site Dockerfile:3, signal = curl/HTTP failure exit status, previously_reached = N/A (newly added path; base had no install step), now_receives = sh's exit status (0 on empty stdin); caller = docker build RUN gate, failure NOT distinguishable.

findings.title: Don't discard ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault; parameterize the default
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (public swallow site) + TRIGGER C (contract drift). LoadOrDefault is an exported function whose only semantic content is `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (src/store.go:16), discarding ErrMissing. Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for a missing key (src/store.go:10) and (v, nil) for a present key (src/store.go:12), including a deliberately stored empty string — so the wrapper's failure result is byte-identical to a legitimate value and no caller can ever distinguish them. The name promises 'OrDefault', yet the signature takes no default parameter: the 'default' is hardwired to "", so a caller cannot supply a real default and is forced into `if v != ""` patterns that misread stored-empty as missing (or vice versa). Per the public-swallow carve-out this is a present defect of the API contract itself, independent of the fact that the repo has zero callers today (rg 'LoadOrDefault' matches only the definition). The failure signal previously reached callers of Load as ErrMissing (src/store.go:10); this new public path downgrades it to an ambiguous zero value with no log and no escape hatch.

findings.title: Exported LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for an absent key (src/store.go:10) and ("", nil) for a present key with an empty value (src/store.go:11). LoadOrDefault discards the error (`v, _ := Load`) and returns "" in both cases, so its public signature makes failure and a real stored value indistinguishable. The name additionally promises a 'default' behavior, but no default exists — the returned fallback is just Load's zero-value companion to the discarded error. Per TRIGGER D this is a defect in the shipped public contract itself, independent of current callers: any eventual caller that persists, routes, or validates on the result cannot detect ErrMissing, and presence/absence information in the map is destroyed.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines finish: no WaitGroup, close(results) races and goroutines leak
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run sent every result synchronously, so its exported contract was: when Run returns, all len(jobs) results have been handed to results. The diff keeps that carrier (exported Run(ctx, jobs, results chan<- int)) but the body now spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no synchronization. A caller using the pattern the old body supported — Run(...); close(results); for r := range results — now races Run's straggler goroutines: a goroutine that has not yet executed `results <- j * 2` sends on a closed channel and panics intermittently. A caller that stops reading early (error or ctx cancel) leaves up to len(jobs) goroutines blocked forever on the send — a permanent goroutine leak (the base code confined such blocking to Run's own frame); ctx is still ignored so they are uncancellable. Concurrency is also unbounded (one goroutine per job, no worker cap). The loop-variable capture is handled correctly via the j parameter, so the defect is purely the missing completion barrier.

findings.title: Run now returns before goroutines finish: breaks completion contract, enables send-on-closed-channel panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (97b9e34) sent `results <- j * 2` synchronously in the loop, so when the exported Run() returned, every job was processed and every result delivered, in job order — the caller could safely close(results) right after Run returned. Head spawns an unwaited goroutine per job: Run returns immediately with zero or more sends still pending. Any caller following the old contract (Run(...); close(ch)) now hits 'panic: send on closed channel' nondeterministically; any caller that stops reading early leaks N goroutines blocked on send forever; and results arrive in arbitrary completion order instead of job order, so order-dependent aggregation silently gets wrong data. Run is exported and returns no WaitGroup/error, so callers have no way to re-establish completion semantics — the API contract itself is broken (TRIGGER C: carrier promises synchronous ordered delivery per base semantics; body @src/worker.go:7-9 computes fire-and-forget async sends).

findings.title: Run returns before goroutine sends finish: panic, leak, or partial results
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run sent every result synchronously, so 'Run returned' meant 'all results delivered' and channel back-pressure applied. The new body spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no WaitGroup or completion signal. For an exported API this breaks every caller shape the old semantics permitted: (1) caller closes results after Run returns → any still-blocked goroutine panics 'send on closed channel'; (2) unbuffered results with a consumer that drains fewer than len(jobs) values concurrently → every undrained goroutine blocks forever (leak/deadlock); (3) caller reading results after Run returns (correct before, e.g. with a sufficiently large buffer) now observes only a nondeterministic subset of results — silent data loss with no error.

findings.title: &&→|| in canDeleteRecord lets any non-admin delete any same-tenant record
findings.whyItBreaks: Previous policy: delete required session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. New policy accepts session.isAdmin OR session.tenantId === record.tenantId. Substitution with real shapes from src/permissions.ts:2-9: session {userId:'u2', tenantId:'t1', isAdmin:false}, record {tenantId:'t1', ownerId:'u1'} → old=false, new=true. Every non-admin member of a tenant can now delete ANY record in that tenant, including records they do not own (RecordRef.ownerId exists at src/permissions.ts:8 and is never consulted), a privilege escalation over the prior admin-only gate. Additionally a cross-tenant admin (session.tenantId !== record.tenantId) now returns true where it was previously false, dropping tenant isolation for the destructive delete action in one direction. The function is exported (public contract) and nothing in the repo — no test, doc, or caller — justifies the loosening; if the intent was owner-or-admin deletion, the body should also compare record.ownerId === session.userId.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord && -> || removes both privilege and tenant-isolation gates
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId: deletion required admin privilege AND tenant match, so tenant isolation applied even to admins. The new || makes either condition sufficient, introducing two distinct bypasses: (1) any authenticated non-admin user of tenant T can now delete ANY record in tenant T (RecordRef.ownerId is never consulted, so users can delete other users' records, including system/audit records), and (2) an admin of tenant A can now delete records in tenant B, breaching cross-tenant data isolation that the base code explicitly enforced. This is an unguarded authorization bypass on a destructive action (deletion = unrecoverable data loss), with no compensating check, test, or justification anywhere in the repo (the file is the repo's entire source).

findings.title: Authz gate weakened: non-admins can delete others' records; admins cross-tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The && → || flip substitutes to concrete wrong behavior on both branches. (1) session={userId:'u2',tenantId:'t1',isAdmin:false}, record={tenantId:'t1',ownerId:'u1'} → old: false (rejected); new: true — a non-admin user can delete a record owned by a different user in the same tenant; RecordRef.ownerId (src/permissions.ts:9) exists precisely to distinguish ownership and is still never consulted, so no ownership check backs the new non-admin allow path. (2) session={userId:'a1',tenantId:'t1',isAdmin:true}, record={tenantId:'t2',ownerId:'u9'} → old: false; new: true — an admin can now delete records in a foreign tenant, breaking the tenant isolation the old predicate enforced even for admins. canDeleteRecord is the module's exported deletion authorization API (only tracked file in the repo), so this loosened predicate IS the product's delete policy; any consumer trusting it now authorizes cross-owner and cross-tenant destructive deletes. No test, doc, or changelog in the repo justifies the escalation.

findings.title: parseSettings catch-all swallows errors; updateFontSize then overwrites valid settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts JSON.parse SyntaxError and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation throws into a silent return of DEFAULTS, with no logging and no signal distinguishing corruption from a legitimately-stored defaults file. Verified consumer: updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) feeds the result straight into save(). Substitution with raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"oops"}': old code threw 'bad fontSize' before save(), leaving the stored file untouched; new code returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14} and save() persists '{"theme":"light","fontSize":N}' — the user's valid 'dark' theme is silently destroyed and the corruption is never surfaced. As an exported API, parseSettings now forces every caller to conflate corrupt input with real defaults.

The new catch at src/settings.ts:14-15 swallows three distinct error signals — JSON.parse SyntaxError, 'bad theme', and 'bad fontSize' (thrown at lines 11-12) — and returns {...DEFAULTS}, making corrupt input indistinguishable from a user who legitimately chose defaults. Concrete live-path substitution in the exported caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22): with raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"big"}' (partially valid file), base behavior threw 'bad fontSize' (base line 11) before save() ran, so the file stayed intact and the corruption surfaced; head behavior returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14}, then save(JSON.stringify(...)) at line 22 silently writes theme:'light' over the user's valid theme:'dark'. findings.title: Bare catch silently maps invalid settings to DEFAULTS, hiding failure from callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` swallows two distinct signals: (1) JSON.parse syntax errors (src/settings.ts:10) and (2) the function's own deliberate validation throws "bad theme"/"bad fontSize" (src/settings.ts:11-12, now inside the try). The not-a-bug carve-outs do not apply: the fallback is not documented as contract anywhere in this repo and failure is neither logged nor distinguishable at any decision point.

findings.title: builtFrom and artifacts now come from different refs — report lies about provenance
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport previously resolved one commit (build.ref(branch)) and used it for both builtFrom and artifactsAt. After this change, builtFrom = build.ref(branch) (line 12) but artifacts = build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")) (lines 13-14). Substitution: for branch="main" with ref("main")="abc123" and ref("verified")="def456", the returned report is { builtFrom: "abc123", artifacts: artifactsAt("def456") } — the report asserts the artifacts came from abc123 when they came from def456. Any consumer of the exported BuildReport (e.g. audit/release tooling keying on builtFrom) cannot detect the mismatch, and the branch parameter silently no longer determines the artifacts, drifting the public contract of buildReport.

findings.title: buildReport pairs artifacts from "verified" ref with builtFrom from caller's branch

The report asserts it was built from abc123 while listing artifacts of def456. The BuildReport contract (src/report.ts:6-9) has only these two fields, so the only sound reading is that artifacts correspond to builtFrom; the changed body breaks that pairing whenever ref(branch) !== ref("verified"), which is the normal case (main, feature branches). Additionally, for any branch whose build has no "verified" ref, build.ref("verified") throws or yields a garbage commit where the previous code worked for every valid branch — the caller's explicit `branch` parameter now governs only half the report. Previously both fields came from one commit (src/report.ts:12-13 at d9fb2d7).

findings.title: Report pairs builtFrom from branch ref with artifacts from "verified" ref

The diff adds `verified = build.ref("verified")` and fetches artifacts at `verified` while leaving `builtFrom: commit`. For every branch whose ref differs from "verified", the exported BuildReport asserts it was built from `commit` but lists artifacts of a different commit — consumers reading the report as 'artifacts of builtFrom' receive the wrong artifact set with no error signal. The half-applied change (builtFrom not switched to `verified`) shows the pairing was broken, not intentionally redesigned.

findings.title: Removed .slice(0, limit): limit parameter no longer caps results
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 still promises 'at most `limit` entries', but the new body returns `[...all].reverse()` unbounded whenever limit > 0 — the limit argument is only consulted for the `<= 0` early return. The relying caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9-11) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and pre-allocates `new Array<string>(20)`, then copies page into it with `out[i] = page[i]` for i < page.length; with >20 entries the write past index 19 extends `out`, so renderFeed returns all entries (e.g. 25 in → length 25) instead of a 20-entry page. Any external caller of this exported API passing a positive limit likewise gets the full list.

The cap — the function's entire reason for taking `limit` — is silently gone on the only path anyone uses.

findings.title: entry-count header includes stale entries that rows now omit
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now renders rows only for non-stale entries (live, line 20) but still passes unfiltered entries.length to headerLines (line 22), so '# entry-count' (line 15) reports the total including stale entries while the manifest body lists fewer rows. Before this diff, entry-count always equaled the number of rendered rows; after it, any manifest containing a stale entry is self-inconsistent, and any consumer parsing entry-count to size/validate row reads gets a count that does not match the data.

Substitution: entries=[a(stale:false), b(stale:true)] → header emits `# entry-count: 2` while only 1 row is rendered. Any consumer that trusts the header count (validation, pagination, 'manifest complete' checks) now sees a declared count that never matches the payload whenever a stale entry exists — an invariant of the exported function's output broken by this change.

findings.title: Header entry-count includes stale entries excluded from rendered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest filters stale entries out of the rendered rows (line 20) but still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length) with the UNFILTERED array (line 22). Substitution: entries = [{path:'a',size:1,stale:true},{path:'b',size:2,stale:false}] → header emits `# entry-count: 2` (line 15) while the body contains only 1 data row. Before this diff, count always equaled row count (rows = entries.map). After it, every manifest containing at least one stale entry — precisely the scenario this change introduces handling for — declares an entry-count that does not match its body. Any consumer that parses `# entry-count` to validate completeness or detect truncation of the manifest will now see a false mismatch on manifests with stale entries. This is contract drift on an exported function's output header: carrier `# entry-count: ${count}` promises the number of entries in the manifest; the body supplies entries.length instead of live.length.

Every multi-tenant read after the first tenant caches a given name receives another tenant's setting — a cross-tenant data leak and wrong-value core-path failure, deterministic on every second-and-later tenant.

findings.title: invalidate() drops required tenantId param, breaking exported API contract

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, serving one tenant's setting value to all tenants

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId — tenants receive each other's settings values

If any setting gates quotas, feature flags, or permissions, tenant B runs under tenant A's policy. invalidate(name) (line 21) compounds it: invalidating one tenant wipes (or, pre-wipe, fails to refresh) the single shared entry for all tenants.

findings.title: invalidate() drops required tenantId param — breaking exported signature change

findings.title: Await inside check-then-act lets concurrent reserves oversell the last unit
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version of reserve() was fully synchronous, so in Node's single-threaded loop the read-check-decrement (stock.get -> remaining<=0 guard -> stock.set) was atomic. This diff inserts `await this.store.save(sku, remaining - 1)` (src/inventory.ts:17) between the guard and the decrement. The await yields the event loop, creating an interleaving point: with stock=1, call A reads remaining=1, passes the guard, and suspends on save; call B then reads remaining=1 (stock not yet decremented), also passes the guard, and suspends; both resume, both set stock to 0, and both resolve true. Two callers are told a unit was reserved when only one existed — a silent oversell, and store.save was invoked with the same stale value 0 twice. This is the core workflow of a class whose job is reservation against a durable store, and it is introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Await between stock check and decrement lets concurrent reserves oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `reserve` was fully synchronous, so read-check-write was atomic in the single-threaded event loop. This diff inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between the check (line 16) and the write (line 18), suspending the method after the check. Substitution with stock=1: call A reads remaining=1, passes the check, suspends at the await; call B then reads remaining=1 (map not yet decremented), passes the same check; both resume, both return true. With stock=5 and 3 concurrent calls, all three read 5, all save `4` to the store, and the map is set to 4 once — three callers are told a reservation succeeded while only one unit was debited. Every concurrent caller (the normal usage pattern for a `Promise<boolean>` API) can now oversell or under-debit inventory; this regression is introduced solely by the changed lines.

findings.title: Await inserted before stock decrement makes reserve() racy: concurrent calls double-sell
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, reserve() was fully synchronous, so its read (line 15) → guard (line 16) → write (line 18) sequence was atomic under JS's single-threaded execution. The diff makes the method async and inserts `await this.store.save(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 17) between the read and the write, introducing a yield point. Interleaving: caller A reads remaining=1, passes the guard, awaits save (yields); caller B then reads the still-undecremented stock (1), passes the guard, awaits save, sets stock=0, returns true; A resumes, sets stock=0 again, returns true. Two reservations are honored and `save(sku, 0)` is persisted for a single unit; with remaining=N, K concurrent calls all persist and return N-1 with only one decrement applied. The method returns a Promise precisely so callers can invoke it concurrently, so the lost-update window is on the method's intended happy path. If `save` rejects after B already persisted, A's rejection leaves memory intact but B's reservation already consumed the unit — failure handling is per-caller while the stock invariant is shared.

findings.title: Unit change to backoff() missed caller retry.ts — sleeps are now 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from returning seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)). Its caller src/net/poll.ts:4 was updated to drop the *1000 conversion and is now equivalent. But the other caller src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still executes `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, where sleep() takes ms (retry.ts:3). Substitution: a=0 → 1000*1000 = 1,000,000ms ≈ 16.7min (was 1s); a=1 → 2,000,000ms ≈ 33min (was 2s); a=5 → 30,000,000ms ≈ 8.3h (was 30s). For attempts=6 the loop's worst-case total delay balloons from ≤ ~63s to ~61,000s ≈ 17h before the final `throw lastErr` (retry.ts:15) — any transient failure followed by retry now stalls the job for hours, a broken retry workflow.

findings.title: retry.ts still treats backoff() as seconds: sleeps 1000x too long after ms migration
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff changes backoff()'s unit from seconds to milliseconds (min(30, 2**a) → min(30000, 2**a * 1000)) and updates schedulePoll accordingly. But the second caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12 (`await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`), was not updated. Substituting real values: attempt=0 previously slept min(30,1)*1000 = 1,000 ms; now it sleeps min(30000, 1000)*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min). attempt>=5 previously capped at 30,000 ms (30 s); now 30,000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h). Every failing call to retry() now blocks its caller for minutes-to-hours between attempts instead of seconds — a broken retry workflow introduced by the changed line.

findings.title: backoff() now returns ms but retry.ts still multiplies by 1000 (1000× delay inflation)
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR changes backoff()'s return unit from seconds to milliseconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt) -> Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and updates one caller (src/net/poll.ts:4) to stop multiplying by 1000, but the other caller src/jobs/retry.ts:12 was not updated and still executes sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). Substituting real values: attempt 0 -> backoff()=1000 -> sleep(1_000_000 ms) ≈ 16.7 min (was 1 s); attempt 5 -> backoff()=30_000 (capped) -> sleep(30_000_000 ms) ≈ 8 h 20 min (was 30 s). Every failed retry now stalls 1000× longer between attempts, silently breaking the retry workflow. TypeScript cannot flag it since both sides are number.

findings.title: Save() now discards the f.Close() error the old code propagated
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ended with `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), so a close failure reached the caller as a non-nil error. Head adds `defer f.Close()` (store/save.go:13), whose return value is dropped, and ends with `return w.Flush()` (store/save.go:20). On filesystems where Close reports delayed write failures (NFS/SMB/FUSE, and any case the OS surfaces at close), Save now returns nil for a save that did not durably complete — the exported API conflates 'failed close' with 'saved', and every caller is forced to treat data loss as success. This is a removed error-propagation branch on a public path (TRIGGER D); it is a present contract defect regardless of there being no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: Save() now discards f.Close() error; failed close reports success

The head version closes via `defer f.Close()` (line 13) whose error is dropped, and returns only `w.Flush()` (line 20). Close is where delayed write-back failures surface (NFS/FUSE writeback errors, ENOSPC/quota at close), so on such a failure Save now returns nil: the caller cannot distinguish 'saved' from 'save lost data' and will treat the write as durable. This is a removed error-propagation branch on an exported API (no in-repo callers yet, rg-verified — the defect is the contract itself).

findings.title: defer f.Close() swallows close errors that Save previously returned
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (c61913c) the success path was `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), so an error from Close — where ENOSPC/EIO can still surface after Flush succeeds on NFS close-to-open, FUSE, or delayed-allocation filesystems — propagated to the caller. The diff replaces this with `defer f.Close()` and `return w.Flush()`, so a close failure after successful writes now returns nil: every caller is forced to conflate 'file durably saved' with 'close failed, file possibly incomplete', and will persist/report the save as real. Save is exported from package store (the module's public API), making the unusable contract itself the defect; error is discarded unconditionally, not even logged.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window: range(start, end - 1) drops last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code iterated `range(start, end)`; the refactor to `range(start, end - 1)` makes every non-empty page one row short, and a page whose window is a single row renders empty. findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window drops last row of every page

Substituting real values: rows=[r0..r4], page_size=2 → page_count=3; page 0: start=0, end=2, range(0,1) yields [r0] (r1 lost); page 2: start=4, end=min(6,5)=5, range(4,4) yields [] so the entire final page is empty even though page_count reports 3 pages. A 1-row dataset (end=min(page_size,1)=1) renders completely empty. Consumers render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) inherit this, so summarize silently omits the last row of every page and emits blank pages for single-row pages — user-visible data loss in rendered output with no error signal.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page via range(start, end - 1)
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor changed the collection loop from the base's correct `range(start, end)` to `range(start, end - 1)`, so the half-open window [start, end) computed by _window_bounds (lines 19-20) is iterated one row short. Substitution: rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_size=3 → page_count=2 (line 14); page 0: bounds (0,3) → collects [a,b] instead of [a,b,c]; page 1: bounds (3,5) → collects [d] instead of [d,e]. summarize/render_page therefore emit pages that silently omit one row per page (and a final page of a single row renders empty), while _format_row keeps global numbering contiguous — the omission is undetectable in the output. This contradicts page_window's own docstring promise ('Rows belonging to page_index') and is a silent data-loss regression for every consumer of render_page/summarize.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code returned entry.value only when fresh (`elapsed < ttlMs`) and deleted+returned null when expired. This diff flips `<` to `>`, so both branches now do the opposite: a FRESH entry (e.g. storedAt 100ms ago, ttlMs 60000: 100 > 60000 is false) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and `return null` — every fresh cached value is destroyed and reported as a miss on its first read. An EXPIRED entry (elapsed 70000 > 60000 is true) returns the stale value, and the delete on line 21 is unreachable for expired entries, so stale data is served forever and never evicted. Any consumer of TtlCache now receives stale data indefinitely and can never get a fresh value back.

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips every second consecutive done job
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach derives its next index from the live array; splice(index, 1) shifts later elements left, so the element that moves into the just-visited index is never visited. Substitution with the base-equivalent input [{id:"a",done:true},{id:"b",done:true}]: forEach visits index 0, splices (array becomes [{id:"b",done:true}]), then advances to index 1 which is now out of range — job "b" is done yet survives the prune. Same for [x,done,done]: after splice(1,1) the array is [x,done] and the next visit (index 2) is out of range. Base behavior (jobs.filter(job => !job.done)) removed ALL done jobs; the replacement returns a wrong result for any input containing adjacent done jobs.

findings.title: pruneDone silently mutates caller's array; filter purity removed
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `pruneDone` returned a new array (filter) and left its argument untouched; the new implementation splices the input in place while keeping the identical `Job[]` return signature, so no caller can detect the change. Substitution: const src=[{id:"a",done:true}]; pruneDone(src) leaves src.length === 0 — the caller's original list was destroyed. Any caller holding a second reference to the input (e.g. the full job list kept for display after pruning a working copy, or vice versa) silently loses its data. This is a public exported API: the aliasing change is a behavioral break for every eventual caller, not just hypothetical ones.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check evicts fresh entries and serves stale ones forever
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from < to >. For a fresh entry (Date.now()-storedAt <= ttlMs) the branch is false, so control falls through to entries.delete(key); return null — every fresh cached value is destroyed on first read and get() misses. For an expired entry (elapsed > ttlMs) the branch is true and entry.value is returned, so stale values are served indefinitely and the delete line can never run for them. Substitution: ttlMs=1000, set('k','v'), get('k') immediately returns null (should return 'v'); after 2000ms get('k') returns 'v' (should return null).

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips the element after each removed job
findings.whyItBreaks: jobs.forEach + jobs.splice(index,1) shifts every later element left by one, but forEach still advances its internal index, so the element that moves into the removed slot's index is never visited. Substitution: [{id:'a',done:true},{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}] → splice at index 0 yields [b(done), c]; forEach next visits index 1 (c); b is skipped and survives. pruneDone returns [b(done), c] instead of [c] — done jobs adjacent to another done job are never pruned, breaking the function's sole purpose.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array instead of returning a new one
findings.whyItBreaks: Base implementation used Array.prototype.filter, which returns a fresh array and leaves the input untouched; the head implementation splices the input array in place and returns the same reference (pruneDone(x) === x). Any caller following the established contract — e.g. `const remaining = pruneDone(allJobs)` while retaining allJobs — now has its array silently corrupted, and (per the adjacent-skip bug) corrupted incorrectly. This is an exported public function, so the purity change is an API contract break even though the repo has no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from < to >. Now an entry older than ttlMs (expired) returns entry.value, so stale data is served indefinitely — each read re-arms the expired entry instead of deleting it. A fresh entry (age <= ttlMs) falls through to entries.delete(key) and returns null, so valid cached values are destroyed and reported as misses on first legitimate read. Base behavior at 1f57af7 was correct.

findings.title: Splice inside forEach skips adjacent done jobs and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach visits indices 0,1,2,... regardless of splices. Removing index i shifts element i+1 into slot i, and the next iteration then reads i+1, skipping it. For [done, done, keep]: i=0 splices out job0 -> [done, keep]; i=1 sees 'keep' (not done); the second done job is never removed, so pruneDone returns jobs that still contain done entries. Additionally the base version used filter and returned a new array; this version mutates the caller's array in place (partially, per the skip), so any caller retaining the original array observes corrupted data — a silent contract change on an exported function whose name promises all done jobs are pruned.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty array after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. For `rows = []`, `[].reduce((s, r) => s + r.amount, 0)` returns 0 (initial value, no throw), so the function now computes `0 / 0 === NaN` where the base commit returned 0. NaN silently poisons every downstream consumer (display, persistence, further arithmetic) instead of yielding a usable number — a wrong value on a legitimate, previously-handled input, on an exported function.

findings.title: busiest sorts the caller's array in place (defensive copy dropped)
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort mutates in place (ES2019+ makes it stable, not non-mutating; toSorted is the copy variant), so every call to busiest reorders the caller's array descending by amount. Callers that read `rows` afterwards (rendering in original order, recomputing stats, caching) observe silently permuted data; if the array is frozen, the sort throws TypeError (ES modules are strict mode). The base commit deliberately copied first.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN after empty-array guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was deleted. For an empty array, `rows.reduce((sum,row)=>sum+row.amount, 0)` yields 0, then `return total / rows.length` computes 0/0 = NaN. Substitution: rows=[] → total=0 → 0/0=NaN. NaN is still typed `number`, so no compiler or type-level signal flags it; any consumer that sums, displays, formats, or persists the average gets a poisoned NaN instead of the previously returned 0. This is a behavior regression on a legitimate input (empty dataset) of an exported function.

findings.title: busiest() mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body copied before sorting (`const ranked = [...rows].sort(...)`); the new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly. `Array.prototype.sort` mutates in place, so calling the exported `busiest(rows)` now silently reorders the caller's array by descending amount. Any caller that retains and reuses `rows` after the call (render order, iteration order, subsequent indices) observes corrupted data with no error. The dropped defensive copy changes the function from pure to side-effecting.

findings.title: averageAmount now returns NaN for empty input instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. For rows=[] the reduce still yields 0 (initial value 0 is passed), then line 8 computes 0 / 0 = NaN. The return type is still `number`, so TypeScript will not flag it; every caller silently receives NaN, which poisons downstream arithmetic, renders as "NaN", and can break persistence/validation that expects a finite number. The documented/previous behavior (0 for empty input) regressed silently on an exported function.

findings.title: busiest sorts the caller's array in place (dropped defensive copy)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaced `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort mutates in place (per spec, ES2019+), so calling busiest(rows) now reorders the caller's array descending by amount as an invisible side effect. Any caller that reads rows afterwards — rendering in original order, summing, indexing — operates on silently reordered data, and the signature `busiest(rows: Row[]): Row | null` gives no hint of mutation.
