findings.title: Default sort() ranks scores lexicographically; topPlayers returns wrong winners
findings.whyItBreaks: rankScores() calls scores.sort() with no comparator, which compares stringified values, then reverses. For scores=[9,10], n=1: sort() yields [10,9] ("10" < "9" as strings), reverse yields [9,10], so the cutoff at line 15 becomes 9 instead of 10; filter(>=9) keeps both players and slice(0,1) returns the first player in input order — the score-9 player — while base code returned the score-10 player. Similarly for scores=[9,2,10], n=2, cutoff becomes 2, letting a score-2 player onto the top-2 board. The exported formatBoard() (line 20) renders these wrong results to users.

findings.title: Default sort() orders scores lexicographically, breaking top-N ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: The numeric comparator `sort((a, b) => b - a)` was replaced by `scores.sort(); scores.reverse();`. `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings, so scores sort lexicographically, not numerically. Substitution with real values: players=[{a,score:2},{b,score:10}], n=1 → rankScores returns [2,10] ('10'<'2' lexicographically then reversed) → cutoff = scores[0] = 2 (line 15) → filter score>=2 keeps [a,b] → slice(0,1) returns player 'a' with score 2 instead of player 'b' with score 10. Same failure for any mixed digit-length scores (9 vs 10). The exported topPlayers and its only consumer formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) silently publish a wrong leaderboard.

findings.title: Default sort() ranks scores lexicographically — wrong top-n cutoff for multi-digit scores
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code sorted numerically descending with `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)`. The new `rankScores` (lines 6-10) replaces it with `scores.sort()` (line 8), which compares the string representations of numbers, then `scores.reverse()` (line 9). For scores [2, 10, 12] the result is [2, 12, 10], not [12, 10, 2]. `topPlayers` (line 14) relies on this array for the cutoff at line 15 (`scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]`). Substitution, n=2, scores [2,10,12]: new cutoff = 12 → filter keeps only score 12 → leaderboard returns 1 entry and wrongly drops the score-10 player (base returned [12, 10]). Substitution, n=1, players [{B,5},{A,12}]: new cutoff = 5 → filter keeps both → slice(0,1) returns B(5), declaring the wrong winner (base returned A(12)). Any score mix crossing digit-length boundaries (1- vs 2-digit, negative numbers) yields wrong winners or dropped entries via the exported `topPlayers`, which also feeds user-visible `formatBoard` (line 20).

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison (timing attack via ==)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing character, so comparison time leaks the length of the matching prefix of the HMAC hexdigest. `verify` is the sole authentication gate for webhooks: `handle` (app/webhook.py:13-16) returns the processor's result with status 200 when `verify` passes and 401 otherwise. A remote attacker can exploit the timing signal with crafted candidate signatures to recover the valid signature byte-by-byte and forge authenticated webhook requests — exactly the attack compare_digest exists to prevent (CWE-208). This is a direct regression introduced by this change; the old code was correct.

findings.title: Timing attack: compare_digest reverted to `==` in webhook auth
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only authentication gate for webhook payloads (app/webhook.py:14 — a passing check leads to processor(payload) with status 200; failing gets 401). The base version compared the computed HMAC-SHA256 hex digest to the supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. This diff replaces it with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`; CPython str equality short-circuits at the first differing character (plus an early length check), so response time reveals how many leading hex characters of the expected digest are correct. An attacker replaying many crafted requests against this endpoint can statistically recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and then forge valid signatures — the exact attack class compare_digest exists to prevent (CWE-208). This is a direct regression of a security control on a changed line, not unchanged code or a hypothetical refactor.

findings.title: verify() uses == instead of hmac.compare_digest, enabling timing attack on signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code compared the computed HMAC to given_signature with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time). The diff replaces it with plain ==, whose runtime depends on the number of matching leading characters. verify() is the sole gate for handle()'s 401/200 decision (app/webhook.py:14), so response timing over the network leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker has guessed. A remote attacker can recover the correct signature byte-by-byte and then forge authenticated webhook payloads — the exact side channel compare_digest exists to close.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; ledger can commit without balances
findings.whyItBreaks: Base d48b674 executed the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs inside `with db.transaction():`, so the three writes committed or rolled back atomically. Head splits them: `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (committed at line 22's block exit), while `_apply_balances` runs at line 23 outside it. If either UPDATE then fails (connection drop, constraint, process crash between the commit and the updates, or between the two updates), the ledger permanently records a transfer whose balances were never (or only half) applied — persisted divergence between ledger and accounts, and any caller retrying after the raised exception inserts a duplicate ledger row. This reintroduces exactly the partial-write/lost-update window the transaction existed to prevent.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; transfer no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (292d3cc), the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs executed inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so a failure anywhere rolled everything back. The refactor commits `_record_ledger` in its own transaction (line 22-23) and then runs `_apply_balances` (line 24) outside any transaction. Concrete failure paths: (1) crash or error after the ledger commit but before/during `_apply_balances` permanently persists a ledger row that says money moved while balances did not — any ledger-based reconciliation or replay later re-moves the money; (2) if the debit UPDATE persists but the credit UPDATE fails (connection drop, constraint), money vanishes from `from_acct` with a committed ledger entry claiming a completed transfer; (3) on `_apply_balances` raising, the caller correctly sees an exception and retries, but the first ledger row is already durable, so the retry inserts a second ledger row and moves money twice. The committed ledger and account balances can no longer be reconciled; this is irreversible money loss/corruption on the module's core path.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; transfer no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (9c436f1) the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs executed inside `with db.transaction():`, so any failure rolled back all three writes. In head, line 23 `_record_ledger(...)` is the only statement inside the `with` block; line 24 `_apply_balances(...)` is dedented to function scope and runs outside the transaction. Consequences: (1) the ledger insert is committed on `with`-block exit BEFORE any balance changes, so a crash or error at line 24 persists a ledger row for a transfer that never moved money; (2) the debit and credit UPDATEs run as separate implicit transactions, so a failure between them (lock timeout, crash, to-account row missing) commits the debit without the credit — money is destroyed — and no rollback restores the committed ledger row or debit. On a money-transfer path this is silent data corruption, not just an unclean error. `_apply_balances` still raises on failure, so callers see an exception yet the persisted state is already half-done and irreversible.

findings.title: billingDay switches UTC date to host-local TZ, changing results per environment
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. For any instant where the local calendar date differs from the UTC date (e.g. 2024-03-15T00:30:00Z in TZ=America/New_York: old output '2024-03-15', new output '2024-03-14'), the returned billing day silently shifts by one day. The value is now a function of the host's ambient TZ env var, so two deployment environments (UTC container vs local dev box, or servers in different zones) disagree about which billing day an event belongs to, and sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8, which composes this function) returns different answers for the same pair of instants depending on where it runs. Day-key values computed before this change and persisted by any downstream consumer no longer match values computed after deployment for boundary instants, mis-attributing charges to the wrong billing day. If a non-UTC billing timezone was the intent, it must be an explicit parameter, not implicit host-local time.

findings.title: billingDay silently switches from UTC to host-local timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite of billingDay replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, changing the day boundary from UTC to the host's local timezone while reading as a pure cleanup (helper extraction). Substitution: at=2024-06-01T23:30:00Z on a UTC+2 host — base code returns '2024-06-01', new code returns '2024-06-02'. Downstream, sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8, the only in-repo reader) flips from true to false for at=2024-06-01T21:00Z vs 23:30:00Z on UTC+2 (23:00 local 06-01 vs 01:30 local 06-02), so any 'same billing day' check (dedup, per-day limit reset) changes classification for identical instants. Additionally, any billing-day string persisted under the base implementation no longer matches newly computed values for boundary-day records after upgrade (migration/upgrade breakage), and the output is now environment-dependent — identical inputs yield different billing days per deployment region/host TZ config. There is no doc, test, or config in the repo pinning an intent to bill in server-local time, and server-local TZ is not a correct basis either way (it should be UTC for stability or an explicit per-customer zone).

findings.title: billingDay now uses local-time getters, silently changing day bucketing
findings.whyItBreaks: base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; head swaps them for getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned billing day now depends on the host timezone instead of UTC. Substitution: for `new Date("2024-03-15T02:30:00Z")` on a host in America/New_York, base yields "2024-03-15" but head yields "2024-03-14" — every instant within the UTC-offset window around midnight is reclassified. Consequences: (1) billing events land on the wrong day (money-impacting bucket shift), (2) two replicas with different TZ settings classify the same instant into different days, so sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) gives inconsistent answers across environments, and (3) any day keys persisted under the old UTC semantics are silently incompatible with new ones on upgrade. The repo contains no test, doc, or migration note indicating local-time billing is intended.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenant: same-named accounts across tenants collide and leak profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map shared by every call to the exported readProfile. The diff changes the key from `${tenant}:${account}` to bare `account`, but the function still scopes accounts by tenant (it passes both to fetchProfile and returns Profile.tenant). Precondition substitution: call readProfile('t1','billing',f1) → memo.set('billing', profile_t1) @line 18; then readProfile('t2','billing',f2) → memo.get('billing') @line 15 hits, `if (cached)` @line 16 takes the cache-hit branch, f2 is never invoked, and the caller asking for tenant t2 receives profile_t1 with tenant==='t1' — wrong-tenant data returned and the correct fetch permanently suppressed for the process lifetime. This breaks tenant isolation for any two tenants sharing an account identifier.

findings.title: Cache key ignores tenant: same account in different tenants collides and leaks the wrong profile
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map shared by all callers (src/profile.ts:7), and `readProfile`'s cache domain is the (tenant, account) pair — `fetchProfile` takes both args (src/profile.ts:12) and `Profile.tenant` exists precisely because profiles are tenant-scoped (src/profile.ts:2). Keying by `account` alone means the first tenant to fetch a given account slug poisons the entry for every other tenant: a subsequent `readProfile("tenantB", "acct", fetch)` hits `memo.get("acct")` (src/profile.ts:14-16), never calls `fetchProfile`, and returns tenant A's Profile — with `profile.tenant === "tenantA"` — to the tenantB caller. Cross-tenant data exposure plus wrong data; the previous `${tenant}:${account}` key made failure and hits tenant-local. The bug is in the exported function itself; no in-repo caller is needed to demonstrate it, and any multi-tenant caller hits it deterministically on the second tenant.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant cache collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map (src/profile.ts:7) shared by all callers. readProfile('tenantA','acct1',f) caches under key 'acct1'; a later readProfile('tenantB','acct1',f) hits `memo.get('acct1')` at line 15 and returns tenantA's Profile without ever calling fetchProfile for tenantB. The returned object's own `.tenant` field ('tenantA') contradicts the requested tenant, so any caller observes wrong-tenant data — a cross-tenant data swap/leak, not merely a stale entry.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: On base, load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) @src/store.ts:4 and the signal propagated to the caller, letting callers detect and report a missing key (and making loadAll abort its batch on the first missing key). The new catch-all `catch { return ""; }` @src/store.ts:6-7 discards that signal and substitutes "" — which Map<string,string> can legitimately contain. Substitution: loadAll(["k"], new Map([["k",""]])) and loadAll(["k"], new Map()) now both return [""]; failure and success are byte-identical. Any caller that previously relied on the throw (error handling, key-existence checks, batch abort) silently proceeds with "" and can persist or report the fallback as real data. The bare catch also discards any other error raised inside the try, not just the missing-key error. This is an exported public API: every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value — the defect ships now, independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns "" instead
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`), which propagated to the caller and named the missing key; loadAll() (src/store.ts:11-12) inherited that fail-fast behavior via Array.map. Now the added unfiltered `catch { return ""; }` converts that failure into an empty string. Since the store is Map<string, string>, "" is a legitimately storable value (store.set(k, "") is valid), so callers cannot distinguish 'key missing' from 'value is empty string' — and the catch is unfiltered, so even a TypeError from a non-Map store argument becomes "". load is exported: every eventual consumer is forced to treat failure as a real value, e.g. loadAll(["a","missing"], m) now returns ["<a>", ""] and the caller can neither detect nor report the missing key that was previously announced by name.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns "", conflating failure with a real value
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D. The diff wraps the existing throw in a catch-all that returns "". `store` is a Map<string, string>, so "" is a legitimate storable value: a caller can no longer distinguish 'key missing' from 'key present with empty-string value'. Previously the error propagated out of the exported function to the caller (previously_reached=caller of load, base src/store.ts:3); now that point receives "". The exported consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12) is affected: loadAll(['a','missing'], s) used to throw loudly; it now silently returns ['<val>', ''], and even positional inspection cannot tell which entries are failures. As an exported swallow site this is a present contract defect — every eventual caller is forced to treat failure as a real value, and any caller that persists or reports the result will act on the fallback as if it were data.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all errors and returns void — failure indistinguishable from success
findings.whyItBreaks: Newly added public export retryBackground discards every error thrown by fn: catch { continue; } (lines 27-28) drops the error without logging or storing it, and the function returns void. After the call, a caller cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded' from 'all retries exhausted', 'deadline hit before first attempt' (line 23 returns early), or 'zero iterations ran because retries was 0/undefined' (line 22 loop never entered). Failure and the silent no-op are both observed as a plain return, so any caller that must know whether the background work happened is forced to conflate total failure with success. This is an added public path with an unusable error contract — the defect ships now regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Shared Config splits attempt count across maxAttempts/retries, read by different functions
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff adds required field `retries` (src/retry.ts:3) to the Config type shared by both exported helpers, then adds retryBackground reading only `retries` (src/retry.ts:22) while the existing retry keeps reading only `maxAttempts` (src/retry.ts:9). Substitution with one shared config: retry(fn, {maxAttempts:3, retries:10, timeout:5000}) performs at most 3 attempts; retryBackground(fn, same) performs up to 10. Nothing in the type, names, or compile-time checks signals the divergence — each function silently ignores the other's attempt knob, and any future fix applied to retry will not propagate to the byte-identical copy at lines 20-31. Under the most charitable reading (retries = re-attempts after first try), the defect persists: the shared type forces every retry caller to supply a `retries` value it ignores and every retryBackground caller to supply a `maxAttempts` value it ignores.

findings.title: Field renders value.length instead of the value itself
findings.whyItBreaks: Base rendered `defaultValue={value}`; head renders `` `len=${value.length}` ``. For any existing caller passing a string (e.g. value="hello") the input now displays "len=5". Because the input is uncontrolled (`defaultValue`), forms will display and SUBMIT the length string instead of the user's value — silent data corruption on every pre-existing string usage. This is a direct behavioral regression introduced by the changed line, not a style concern.

findings.title: value: string | number accepted but number branch unimplemented
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop type was widened to `string | number`, promising the component handles numbers, but line 6 computes `value.length` with no `typeof` narrowing. `number` has no `length` property, so under any tsc-based check this is a compile error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number') and the build breaks; under transpile-only toolchains (Babel/esbuild/SWC) it compiles and the newly allowed public path `<Field value={42} />` renders `defaultValue="len=undefined"` — garbage in the field and in whatever the form submits. The public contract promises number support the body does not implement, and the promised behavior directly changes the data a caller receives.

findings.title: value.length is invalid for the newly added number type: renders 'len=undefined'
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop type FieldProps.value was widened to `string | number` (line 2), promising callers the component accepts numbers, but the body computes `value.length` (line 6). Substitution with the newly supported type: value=42 → (42).length === undefined → label = 'len=undefined' → <input defaultValue="len=undefined">. The number branch of the widened contract produces garbage output for any caller. Additionally, `value.length` on type `string | number` is a TypeScript compile error (TS2339), so any tsc-based build/typecheck gate fails. Even for the unchanged string case, behavior silently changed from rendering the value itself to rendering its length, so no caller can display the field's actual value anymore. Exported public component (repo has no other callers yet — verified via rg), so the broken number contract ships in the API now.

findings.title: value.length on string|number union: type error and len=undefined for numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The public exported prop type now promises `value: string | number` accepts numbers (line 2), but line 6 evaluates `value.length` without narrowing. Substituting the newly-admitted value: for `value={42}`, `value.length` is `undefined`, so the input renders the garbage string `len=undefined` as its defaultValue — failure and a real length are indistinguishable to the rendered output. Independently, `value.length` on the `string | number` union is a hard TypeScript property-existence error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), so any TS build/typecheck including this exported file fails; this is a language-level error, independent of strictness flags. Note the change also swaps rendered output from `value` to `len=${value.length}` for existing string callers, so even the previously-valid string path now displays a length label instead of the value.

findings.title: Remove echo that interpolates secrets.TOKEN into workflow log output
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step expands secrets.TOKEN into shell stdout ('echo "deploying with $TOKEN"'), putting the credential into job logs. GitHub only protects this via its runtime exact-match log masking (*** substitution); masking is a safety net, not a contract — job logs are downloadable by anyone with repo read access and retained by log-retention settings. The echo serves no functional purpose (no consumer uses TOKEN; step-scoped env never reaches 'make build'), so the exposure path exists purely for a debug print and should be removed before merge.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into the deploy workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects secrets.TOKEN into the step environment solely to run `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the secret into the workflow's log output. Actions logs are retained and readable by everyone with read access to the repo, and GitHub's secret masking is best-effort only — it does not reliably mask values that are transformed, split, multiline, or non-UTF-8, so any future tweak to the echo bypasses it. The token is also used nowhere else (env is scoped to this step; `make build` at line 13 never sees it), so the step's only real-world effect is exposing the secret.

findings.title: Remove echo of secrets.TOKEN into workflow run logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow triggers on push, so every push materializes secrets.TOKEN and prints 'deploying with $TOKEN' to the run log, which is readable by anyone with read access to the repo (everyone, if public). The only protection is GitHub's automatic exact-match log masking — a best-effort redaction that fails for short or character-trimmed secret values and is bypassed by any future tweak to the echo (substring like ${TOKEN:0:8}, base64/JSON encoding, or shell tracing), at which point the credential is published verbatim. The step also serves no function: the env is scoped to this step only, so make build never receives TOKEN, and nothing else in the repo consumes it. A deploy credential should never be placed on a log-emitting path.

findings.title: git() loses 64MiB maxBuffer; patches >1MiB now crash the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 from the git() spawnSync options (old file line 40), so Node's documented 1MiB default applies. git() is used at src/adapters/github.ts:140 to fetch the full PR patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha`) — output that routinely exceeds 1MiB (lockfiles, generated/minified files, bulk renames). When output exceeds maxBuffer, spawnSync terminates the child with error.code=ENOBUFS and res.status=null, so line 38 (`res.status !== 0`) throws 'git diff ... failed: ' with an empty stderr. Every large-diff PR now ends in 'review failed' + exitCode 1 (lines 182-193) where it previously succeeded up to 64MiB — a direct regression of the runner's core path. The gh()/ghText() wrappers (lines 19, 29) still carry maxBuffer 64MiB, making the removal here inconsistent, not a deliberate policy.

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha reports PR base tip, not the patch's actual base
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.baseSha was changed from mergeBase to baseSha (env PR_BASE_SHA, or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD), line 138), while patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are still computed from mergeBase (line 139). The Bundle contract pairs baseSha with headSha/patch such that diff(baseSha, headSha) == bundle.patch — exactly how the downstream reviewer consumes the bundle. mergeBase == baseSha only while PR_BASE_SHA is an ancestor of headSha; as soon as the base branch advances after the PR fork point (normal in active repos), diff(baseSha, headSha) additionally contains the base branch's own commits reversed/absent relative to the patch. Every consumer that uses baseSha to interpret the review — reading pre-PR file state via `git show baseSha:file`, re-deriving the diff, or building validation commands — now works against a different base than the one the patch context was computed against, producing findings/validations mismatched to the PR. The old code (baseSha: mergeBase) guaranteed the reported base was the patch's true base (a common ancestor); this change breaks that guarantee with no compensating change to patch/changedFiles.

findings.title: git() losing 64MiB maxBuffer fails review of any >1MiB PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's default of 1 MiB. The only unbounded git() call is the full PR patch `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha])` (line 141); a diff over 1 MiB (lockfile/vendor/generated changes — routine in real PRs) makes spawnSync kill the child with ENOBUFS, so res.status is null, `res.status !== 0` throws with empty stderr, and runGithub's catch posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' failure check and exits 1. PRs that reviewed fine at base commit (64 MiB cap) now fail outright; the gh()/ghText() helpers still carry the 64 MiB cap, confirming the git cap was load-bearing, not dead config.

findings.title: Bundle advertises base-branch tip as baseSha while patch uses mergeBase
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 141) and changedFiles (line 142) are computed from mergeBase (merge-base of baseSha and headSha, line 139), but bundle.baseSha now carries baseSha — the PR_BASE_SHA env value, i.e. the base-branch tip. In Actions (where PR_BASE_SHA is set, mirroring PR_HEAD_SHA), whenever the base branch has advanced past the fork point, baseSha ≠ mergeBase and the bundle is self-contradictory: bundle.baseSha..headSha spans commits that are not part of the PR, while patch/changedFiles do not. Any consumer using bundle.baseSha as the diff base (re-deriving the diff, scoping inline comments, fetching base-side content) operates out of PR scope — exactly the wrong-diff bug mergeBase was introduced to prevent. When PR_BASE_SHA is unset, baseSha == mergeBase and the change is a no-op, so the defect is confined to the primary CI path.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): >1MiB patches now throw and escape error handling
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB; on a larger stdout the child is killed (res.status=null, error ENOBUFS), so the guard at line 38 throws. The main consumer is line 140: patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) — the full unified diff of the PR, which for lockfile churn/generated code routinely exceeds 1 MiB but fits the previous 64 MiB buffer. This call executes before the try block at line 176, so the throw escapes runGithub without posting a review or even the failure check-run from the catch at line 182 — CI silently crashes instead of reporting. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers (lines 19, 29) retain maxBuffer 64MiB, showing the limit was deliberate for exactly this output class.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha must be mergeBase: patch/changedFiles are computed from merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are both computed against mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha, but the bundle now carries baseSha (line 138: PR_BASE_SHA env or merge-base of origin/main). Whenever the base branch has advanced since the PR branched — the common case — baseSha != mergeBase, so review(bundle) at line 177 receives a base commit inconsistent with the patch and changed-file set: any base-tree read or git diff baseSha..headSha downstream silently analyzes reverted base-branch commits that are not part of the PR. Additionally, on default shallow actions/checkout runs PR_BASE_SHA may not exist as a local object, so any downstream git operation on bundle.baseSha fails outright, while mergeBase is guaranteed to be an ancestor of HEAD (it just resolved at line 139).

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only`: sandbox pin removed from codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath and feeds an arbitrary prompt via stdin (src/shared/codex.ts:20-30); at base (624d59a) the argv pinned the agent sandbox with `-s read-only`. The head argv drops it, so the sandbox mode now falls back to the codex binary's ambient resolution (config.toml profiles/env or CLI default) instead of being enforced here. In any environment where codex resolves a writable sandbox, this helper now executes a model agent with write access over the target repo; this is exactly the injection-prone execution path (PR-derived prompts) whose read-only boundary was the containment for prompt-injection payloads. No in-repo caller re-adds the flag (rg: runCodex referenced only at its definition), so nothing compensates for the lost guarantee.

findings.title: Dropping '-s read-only' lets codex run with config-dependent write access
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath and a prompt that may embed untrusted repository content. The removed `-s read-only` flag unconditionally pinned the agent to a read-only sandbox; without it, the sandbox mode is taken from ambient codex configuration (`sandbox_mode`), which users commonly set to `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` for interactive development. On any such machine, this invocation silently escalates from 'agent cannot modify anything' to 'agent can write to (and, with danger-full-access, execute against) the repo under review', re-enabling prompt-injection-driven file mutation that the previous line provably prevented. The guarantee changed from 'always read-only' to 'read-only only if the ambient config happens to say so', with no code-level enforcement left.

findings.title: Dropped read-only sandbox lets codex agent mutate the target repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with cwd = an arbitrary `opts.repoPath` and a prompt as stdin. On this path the prompt itself carries untrusted content (PR diffs / code under review), so `-s read-only` was the single unconditional control preventing a prompt-injected agent from writing files or running mutating commands in the target checkout. The diff removes that flag, so the sandbox now comes from ambient state the harness no longer controls: `~/.codex/config.toml` `sandbox_mode` (commonly set to `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` on developer machines), env, or the codex version's default. With any non-read-only effective sandbox, an injected instruction can modify/delete files in the repo under review mid-run — data loss plus review-integrity corruption, since the agent can alter the very content being reviewed (and in the needlefish harness this module is the shared runner for exactly that). Previously guaranteed read-only behavior silently degrades per-machine; the caller (`opts`) offers no way to restore the restriction.

findings.title: Removing merge-base makes diff include reversed base-branch commits when baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code computed mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha (three-dot). The new code diffs baseSha..HEAD (two-dot). These are equivalent only when baseSha is an ancestor of HEAD — true for the unchanged fallback at line 138 (it already yields a merge-base), but NOT guaranteed for the supported env input PR_BASE_SHA (line 138). GitHub's PR base.sha is the current head of the base branch; once main advances after the PR forked, baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD. Substitution: baseSha=diverged base head → git diff baseSha HEAD returns PR changes PLUS the reverse of every commit on base since the fork point. Effect on live consumers of the changed values: patch → bundle.patch → review() now presents deletions of unrelated merged work as PR regressions (spurious changes_requested); changedFiles → changedFileSet @56-58 → changedPaths @141 → inlineComments filter changedPaths.has(f.file) @61-64 now admits files the PR never touched, so findings can be posted inline against lines that don't exist on commit_id=headSha. Silently wrong core output of this adapter whenever the base branch moved. Minimal fix restores the three-dot base.

findings.title: PR diff loses merge-base scoping; includes base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` line normalized the diff to the fork point (three-dot semantics). New code diffs `baseSha..HEAD` directly. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the standard GitHub value (`pull_request.base.sha` = base branch tip, which advances past the fork point), `git diff baseSha HEAD` emits reverse hunks undoing every commit merged to the base branch since the fork, and `changedFileSet` (line 62, `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`) lists files only touched on main — so the review bundle contains changes the PR never made, findings can be posted about them (inlineComments filters by these same polluted changedPaths, line 76), and PR changes that cancel against base changes can silently vanish from review. Additionally, replacing `headSha` with literal "HEAD" means that under default Actions checkout (HEAD = PR-into-base merge commit, PR_HEAD_SHA = PR tip) the reviewed content is the merge commit's tree while the result is attached via `commit_id: headSha` (lines 93, 121) — reviewed content and pinned commit disagree. Only the no-env local path (HEAD = PR tip, baseSha = merge-base) is unchanged.

findings.title: Restore merge-base: diffing baseSha..HEAD leaks base-branch commits into the PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseSha, headSha])` guaranteed the patch contained only PR-introduced changes even when baseSha (PR_BASE_SHA, which CI harnesses set to the base-branch tip, not the merge base — the exact gotcha merge-base calls exist to fix) is ahead of the PR's fork point. After this change, for every file main touched since the PR diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` emits a reverse hunk reverting main's commits to the PR branch's stale state, and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` lists files the PR never modified. Consequences: (1) bundle.patch fed to review() misrepresents the PR, so the model can raise findings or REQUEST_CHANGES against correct code; (2) those spurious paths pass the changedPaths filter in inlineComments (src/adapters/github.ts:78), so inline comments get posted (side RIGHT, line=f.lineStart) on lines that are not part of the real PR diff — GitHub rejects such reviews with 422, the catch falls back to posting without inline comments (silent loss of all inline comments), or worse, comments annotate main's reverted hunks as if the PR changed them. The default path (both env vars unset) is unchanged: baseSha is then already the merge-base of origin/main and HEAD, so old merge-base(baseSha, headSha) === baseSha.

findings.title: String replace values re-enable $-pattern substitution, corrupting prompt content
findings.whyItBreaks: When replace() is given a string replacement, JS interprets $$ as '$', $& as the matched placeholder, and $`/$' as the prompt text before/after the match. bundle.patch and the stringified bundle/findings are free-form PR text (raw diffs of Makefiles/shell/regex code routinely contain $$, $', $&). Base code used function replacers () => value precisely to bypass this; this diff removes them, so any such PR gets a mangled patch/bundle injected into the prompt at lines 27 and 34 — e.g. 'diff --git a/Makefile... echo $$VAR' becomes 'echo $VAR', and $& in a sed example silently becomes '{{PATCH}}' inside the critic prompt, so the model reviews corrupted content.

findings.title: String replacers re-enable $$/$&/$`/$' corruption of prompt content
findings.whyItBreaks: With a string (non-function) replacement, String.prototype.replace interprets special replacement patterns in the replacement text per ECMA-262 GetSubstitution: $$ collapses to a single $, $& expands to the matched literal ({{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}}), $` inserts the prompt prefix, and $' inserts the prompt suffix. The base code used replacer functions (() => value) precisely so the JSON.stringify(bundle), JSON.stringify(candidate), and bundle.patch values were inserted verbatim. The head commit reverts to plain string replacers, so any PR patch or findings JSON containing $$ (Makefile/shell), $' (bash ANSI-C quoting), $& (sed/regex), or $` silently corrupts the prompt: JSON blocks stop parsing, patch text is replaced by template markers or duplicated prompt text, and review()/critic run over mangled input with no error raised — wrong review output on the core path.

findings.title: String .replace() arguments corrupt prompt payload via $ special patterns
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement interprets $$ (→ $), $& (→ the matched placeholder, e.g. '{{PATCH}}'), $` and $' (→ prompt text before/after the placeholder). The base commit used replacer functions (() => ...) precisely so the interpolated text is used literally; this diff removes them. bundle.patch is a git patch, and Makefiles/shell code routinely contain $$ and $' (e.g. 'kill $$', bash $'...'), and findings/JSON quoting the diff can carry $&. Any such sequence silently rewrites the critic's {{PATCH}}/{{FINDINGS}} payload (verified: 'A{{PATCH}}B'.replace('{{PATCH}}','kill $$ | git apply $&') === 'Akill $ | git apply {{PATCH}}B'), so runCodex reviews a corrupted patch and the review result is silently wrong — no error is raised.

findings.title: Stop coercing malformed findings into fabricated P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on every malformed field ('malformed finding: invalid severity/category/lineStart...', missing file/title/whyItBreaks) and normalizeReview(strict=false) dropped unparseable elements. The head version deletes all of it: an invalid or missing severity silently becomes "P1" (line 98) — garbage input is inflated into a high-severity finding that drives verdicts; a missing file becomes "" (line 103) and lineStart/lineEnd become 0 (lines 104-105); a non-numeric lineStart/lineEnd (e.g. "abc") becomes NaN since Number() without isFinite is no longer rejected; a missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (line 99) and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix pass through as "". The returned object still types as Finding, so no consumer can distinguish 'producer emitted malformed data' from 'producer emitted a real P1 about file "" at line 0' — failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate value at every decision point. This is an exported swallow site (TRIGGER D) with the strict=false rejection path also removed (old normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) at base lines 137/155-163; head line 113 takes no strict arg), so the module now has NO path that surfaces a malformed finding. Fabricated P1/empty-anchor findings flow into RawReview.findings as if real.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates a P1 finding from malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: The function previously threw on invalid severity, category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or non-positive line numbers (base lines 96-122), so callers could never receive an invalid Finding. Now every failure is masked: normalizeFinding({severity:"critical", file:"x.ts"}) returns {severity:"P1", category:"bug", file:"", lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, whyItBreaks:"", suggestedFix:""}. A garbage/unparseable finding is indistinguishable from a real one and is inflated to high severity ("P1"), not downgraded. The only visible consumer, normalizeReview (line 131), passes these fabricated findings straight into the public RawReview output, so downstream stages receive a high-severity finding with no file, no line, and empty rationale as if it were a legitimate review result. Failure is no longer detectable at any decision point — the swallow site is the exported contract itself.

findings.title: normalizeReview drops strict parameter, breaking both prior call modes
findings.whyItBreaks: Base signature normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) defined two behaviors: default strict mode threw on malformed findings; strict=false dropped them (base lines 155-165). Head removes the parameter entirely: two-argument callers now fail type-check (arity break), and any JS caller passing strict=false silently changes semantics from 'drop malformed findings' to 'include fabricated findings' — garbage that was previously filtered out now lands in the returned RawReview.findings. Both prior contracts are gone with no compat path in an exported shared module.

findings.title: NaN leaks into lineStart/lineEnd/confidence via unchecked Number() casts
findings.whyItBreaks: Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) only traps null/undefined; a non-numeric string yields NaN: normalizeFinding({file:"a.ts", lineStart:"12a"}) produces lineStart:NaN and lineEnd:NaN (Number(undefined ?? "12a") = NaN), and confidence becomes NaN because Math.min/Math.max propagate it. The base code enforced Number.isFinite on both line fields (base lines 115-121), so this state was unreachable before. Finding.lineStart is typed number, so downstream arithmetic and guards (e.g. lineStart >= 1 anchoring checks, comparisons for comment placement) silently misbehave on NaN (all comparisons false), and JSON.stringify serializes it as null, corrupting the persisted/reported review.

findings.title: Malformed findings silently fabricated as P1/bug/empty-file instead of rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: Base normalizeFinding threw on invalid severity/category/file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix and on non-finite or <=0 lineStart/lineEnd (base lines 96-122, Number.isFinite guards); normalizeReview defaulted strict=true and its strict=false mode dropped invalid findings. Head replaces every rejection with a default: garbage severity becomes "P1" (line 98) — a blocking-severity finding fabricated from unparseable input; invalid category becomes "bug" (100-102) with no case/trim normalization, so "SECURITY" is misclassified as "bug"; missing file becomes "" (103) and lineStart/lineEnd become 0 or NaN (104-105: Number("abc")=NaN, and "abc"??0 bypasses the nullish default, so the removed Number.isFinite guard now lets NaN through). Consumers of the exported Finding can no longer distinguish "model produced a real P1 finding" from "input was garbage" (TRIGGER D: failure mapped to default values, error signal discarded). Removing the strict parameter (normalizeReview, lines 113/131) eliminates both prior safe paths — fail-fast throw and drop-invalid — forcing fabrication on every caller.

findings.title: gh pr view without -R breaks workflow_dispatch repo resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step is the job's FIRST step (line 26); no actions/checkout runs before it, so at execution time the workspace is not guaranteed to be a git checkout of this repo — especially with `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 24), where workspace state is ambient. gh CLI resolves the repository as: -R flag → GH_REPO env → git remotes of cwd; it does NOT read the runner-provided GITHUB_REPOSITORY. Removing `-R "$REPO"` (and the `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` env) leaves no explicit target. On a fresh/cleaned self-hosted workspace there are no remotes, so `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` fails with 'could not determine current repository' and the entire manual-dispatch review path (the documented 'bypasses pull_request webhook' trigger, lines 11-15) aborts at step 1. On a reused/shared self-hosted workspace, leftover remotes from a previous job's checkout can point at a DIFFERENT repository, so the required `pr_number` input is silently resolved against the wrong repo — reviewing the wrong PR or erroring confusingly. The pull_request path (lines 34-36) is unaffected because it never invokes gh. The removed `github.repository` context was the correct, checkout-independent source; nothing in the diff or repo compensates (no GH_REPO set anywhere).

findings.title: gh pr view loses repo context: -R removed before any checkout exists
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) is the job's FIRST step; actions/checkout only runs later (line 42), and `GH_REPO` is not set anywhere in the file. `gh pr view` resolves its repository from, in order: the -R flag (just removed), GH_REPO (absent), then git remotes in the current directory. Substituting on the workflow_dispatch path (the only branch that reaches these lines, since pull_request events short-circuit on non-empty EVENT_HEAD at line 34): a clean runner workspace has no .git, so gh errors with 'could not determine current repository' and every manual-dispatch review fails; on the self-hosted runner (line 23) the workspace persists between runs, so gh falls back to the leftover origin remote — same repo only by coincidence, and the WRONG repo's PR number is queried if the runner is cleaned or shared across repos, producing a review of a mismatched PR (head/base SHAs from a foreign repository fed into checkout at line 45). `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (line 29) provides auth only, never repo context, so removing REPO/-R removed the sole explicit repo anchor.

findings.title: gh pr view without -R cannot resolve repo before checkout; refs silently become empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The `else` branch runs only on workflow_dispatch, and the "Resolve PR refs" step is the job's FIRST step — no actions/checkout has run yet, so the runner workspace is not a git repository (fresh/ephemeral self-hosted runner). gh resolves the target repo from `GH_REPO` (not set anywhere in this workflow — verified), the `-R` flag (just removed), or git remotes in cwd (unavailable at this point); it does NOT read the `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` env var that Actions exports. Both `gh pr view` calls therefore fail on a clean workspace. The failure is also silent: under Actions' default `bash -e -o pipefail` shell, a failed command substitution does not fail the enclosing `echo`, so the step succeeds writing `head=` and `base=` as empty strings to GITHUB_OUTPUT. "Checkout PR head" then gets `ref: ''` (treated as unset → checks out the default branch) and the "Needlefish review" step runs with PR_BASE_SHA='' / PR_HEAD_SHA='' — reviewing the wrong code or erroring downstream instead of failing here. On a stale self-hosted workspace the leftover .git remote can accidentally resolve to this repo, masking the bug intermittently. The removed `-R "${{ github.repository }}"` was the only correct repo source on this path.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors as a valid empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw Error('malformed review output: …') at five guard sites (base lines 115–131) whenever raw was not an object, summary was not a string, or findings/checked/residual_risks were not arrays. The head version deletes every throw and substitutes defaults: non-object raw → {summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []} (lines 115–128). An empty review is a legitimate value (a clean pass with no findings), so failure and success are indistinguishable at every downstream decision point — garbage reviewer output (truncated JSON, prose instead of an object, wrong field types) now yields the same shape as a real passing review and would be persisted/reported as a pass. This is a TRIGGER D swallow on an exported public function: normalizeReview is exported from the sole module of this package, so every eventual caller is forced to accept failure-as-value; the fallback is not part of any documented contract and nothing logs or flags the malformed case.

findings.title: normalizeReview now silently converts malformed review output into an empty 'clean' review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version validated raw review input and threw five distinct errors ('malformed review output: not an object | summary missing or not a string | findings missing or not an array | checked missing or not an array | residual_risks missing or not an array', base lines 115-131). The head version removes every throw and substitutes defaults: null/non-object input → {summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []} (lines 124-129); missing summary → "" (line 125); missing findings/checked/residual_risks → [] (lines 115-123, 127). This module's exported purpose is normalizing LLM review output into RawReview, which feeds ReviewResult.verdict. After this change, garbage/truncated model output is indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings — a caller that derives a verdict from the result will record failure as a clean pass, and no error signal remains anywhere (there is no logging in the file). The fallback is not part of any documented contract. Note the asymmetric design intent preserved in normalizeFinding (lines 94-112): item-level fields are coerced with defaults, but shape-level integrity was enforced by throwing; this PR deletes the entire shape-validation layer.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently converts malformed review output into an empty 'clean' review
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is an exported parser for review output. The base version threw 'malformed review output: ...' for five conditions (raw not an object; summary not a string; findings/checked/residual_risks not arrays), letting callers detect and handle a malformed model response. This diff deletes every throw and substitutes defaults: raw=null → {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} (lines 114-129). Failure is now mapped to a value identical to a legitimately empty/clean review, so any caller (e.g. a review pipeline computing a pass/block verdict from findings, or persisting the review) cannot distinguish 'model returned garbage' from 'review found nothing' — a malformed response is silently reported as a clean pass instead of surfacing an error or triggering retry.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path lost SHA resolution: empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA and wrong checkout ref

On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is null, so: (1) PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA at lines 45-46 resolve to empty strings — the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step's else branch (old lines 39-42) was the sole provider of these values on this path, resolving them via 'gh pr view "$PR_NUM"', and it was removed with no replacement; the CLI at line 47 is still invoked with --pr <input> but now receives empty SHA env vars. (2) Checkout ref at line 29 falls back to github.ref (the branch the workflow was dispatched from, typically the default branch) instead of the PR head SHA that old line 48 checked out — and per the file's own comment (lines 3-4) the PR checkout's src/ IS the review tool, so self-review via dispatch now runs the tool from an unrelated ref. (3) BASE_REF at line 35 defaults to 'main' even when the reviewed PR targets a different base branch (previously resolved via gh pr view as base_ref). Substitution on the live dispatch path yields empty SHAs + wrong checkout + wrong base ref; the pull_request path is unchanged.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path lost PR ref resolution: wrong checkout, empty SHA envs
findings.whyItBreaks: This workflow still declares workflow_dispatch with a required pr_number input (lines 10-14), admits it in the job if (line 24), and still passes --pr ${{ inputs.pr_number }} (line 47), but the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step (old lines 40-42) was the only code that resolved the input PR's refs. On workflow_dispatch github.event.pull_request is empty, so by substitution: checkout ref expression at line 29 evaluates to github.ref (the branch dispatched from, typically the default branch — NOT the PR head), PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA at lines 45-46 export empty strings instead of the PR's base/head SHAs, and BASE_REF at line 35 falls back to 'main' even when the PR targets another branch. Self-review mode explicitly runs the checked-out src as the tool (comment lines 3-5), so a manual dispatch now executes the wrong tool version against the wrong code with no base/head SHAs, and can post PR comments/checks from a bogus diff. The old path either produced the correct refs or failed the job loudly when gh pr view failed; the new path silently proceeds with defaults (swallowed failure signal at lines 29, 45-46).

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git(): 1MiB default kills reviews of large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used to fetch the full patch via `git diff <base> <head>` (src/adapters/local.ts:100), whose output is unbounded PR content fed into bundle.patch. With the explicit `maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64` removed, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default: for any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync kills the child (res.status = null, res.error = ENOBUFS), the `res.status !== 0` check at line 12 throws, and runLocal rejects — the entire review fails for every large PR, which worked at base (64 MiB headroom). The real cause (res.error/ENOBUFS) is also discarded by the error message, so the thrown 'git diff ... failed:' gives operators no hint output size was the trigger. The sibling gh() wrapper (line 36) keeps the 64 MiB buffer, confirming the git() value was deliberate and its removal is inconsistent, not cleanup.

findings.title: Removed maxBuffer reverts git() to 1 MiB default; large diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `spawnSync("git", args, { cwd, encoding: "utf8", maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 })` with `spawnSync("git", args, { cwd, encoding: "utf8" })`, silently falling back to Node's default maxBuffer of 1 MiB. The helper's largest consumer is src/adapters/local.ts:100 — `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` — which captures the full unbounded branch patch (the tool's core review payload). Once stdout exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync kills the child: `res.status` is null (not 0), so the guard at line 12 throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with empty stderr, and nothing in runLocal catches it — the entire review run fails for any PR whose diff is >1 MiB (roughly >25-30k diff lines), a case that worked up to 64 MiB before. The sibling gh() helper at line 36 retains maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, confirming the large-buffer requirement was deliberate in this adapter; the one-line options rewrite dropped it. Line 101 (`diff --name-only`, huge refactor PRs) is affected by the same fix.

findings.title: Restoring maxBuffer: removed cap breaks diffs >1MiB (Node default)
findings.whyItBreaks: git() previously passed maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 to spawnSync; the diff removes it, so the effective limit falls to Node's documented default of 1024*1024 (1MiB). The core input of this adapter is the full patch captured at src/adapters/local.ts:100 via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]). On a diff whose stdout exceeds 1MiB, node:child_process kills the child (SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS), leaving res.status = null; the guard at src/adapters/local.ts:12 (res.status !== 0) then throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr. The entire runLocal review aborts for any PR with a >1MiB diff — a normal input for this tool, not an edge case. The sibling gh() helper (src/adapters/local.ts:33-37) still passes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, proving the 64MiB cap was deliberate for this codebase's large-output commands and that this is a removal regression, not standardization. The failure is loud (throw), not silently swallowed (TRIGGER D not fired): overflow cannot yield status===0, so no truncated patch is ever reviewed.

findings.title: Patch (gh pr diff) and changedFileSet (git diff baseTip..HEAD) now diverge
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, `patch` and `changedFileSet` used the identical diff (`git diff baseSha HEAD`). Now `patch = ghText(["pr","diff",…])` @143 is GitHub's merge-base(base,head)..head diff, while `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` @144 still runs the two-dot `git diff --name-only pr.base.sha HEAD` against the local checkout with base branch TIP. Substitution (head checkout, branch behind base): the two-dot diff renders base-side changes as reversed deletions, so changedPaths gains phantom files absent from `gh pr diff`; a finding on such a file (the reviewer reads repo files and bundle.changedFiles surfaces) passes the inlineComments filter @63, is sent as a review comment on a path not in the PR diff, and GitHub rejects the entire review POST with 422 — the catch at @96 then silently re-posts without ANY inline comments. Converse case (base and PR converge a file to identical content): the path is in `gh pr diff` but not in changedPaths, so its inline comment is silently filtered out @63. bundle.changedFiles also misstates PR scope to the reviewer in these deployments.

findings.title: Patch is now three-dot PR diff but changedFileSet stays two-dot; sets can diverge
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, patch (`git diff baseSha HEAD`, line 139 old) and changedFileSet (`git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`, line 57) were the same two-dot computation, so patch paths == changedPaths by construction. Now patch comes from `gh pr diff` (GitHub's three-dot merge-base..head diff) while changedFileSet still diffs two-dot from pr.base.sha (the base branch TIP). When the base branch has moved since the merge-base (or the checkout is the PR head rather than the Actions merge ref), files changed on main appear in changedPaths but not in the patch. The reviewer receives changedFiles with surfaces (bundle line 171) and can emit a finding on such a path; inlineComments (line 63) then includes a comment on a path absent from the PR diff, the POST /pulls/N/reviews call returns 422, and the pre-existing catch (line 96) silently re-posts the review with ALL inline comments dropped. Conversely a PR-touched file whose content main reconciled back is in the PR diff but filtered out of changedPaths (line 63), silently suppressing its inline comments. Both failure modes were impossible before this change because the two sets were identical.

findings.title: gh pr diff resolves the repo from process CWD, not the `repo`/`cwd` args
findings.whyItBreaks: Every other gh call embeds the repo explicitly in the API path (line 138 `repos/${repo}/pulls/...`), and every git call passes `cwd`; ghText/spawnSync (lines 28-33) passes neither. gh does not honor GITHUB_REPOSITORY — `gh pr diff N` resolves the repo only from GH_REPO or the git remote of the process CWD. runGithub takes `cwd` as a parameter, so CWD ≠ checkout is a supported invocation: (a) CWD outside a clone → gh errors 'could not determine the repository' → the whole review aborts (check run goes 'review failed'); (b) CWD inside a different clone → gh silently returns PR #N of the WRONG repository and the review posts findings derived from the wrong patch onto the target PR — wrong data in, wrong comments out, no error.

findings.title: Self-review mode executes untrusted PR code as the reviewer on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Base pinned all executed tool code to trusted main: the reviewer was a second checkout of frankekn/needlefish@main and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` ran against main's lockfile. The base comment stated the invariant explicitly: 'This prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' This diff deletes that control. Now lines 43-47 check out only the PR head, line 51 runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the PR's own lockfile (executing the full dependency tree's postinstall scripts chosen by the PR), and line 59 runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from that same PR checkout — with GH_TOKEN holding `pull-requests: write` + `checks: write` (L16-19) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (L23). A PR can make its own review say anything (self-approving reviews via --github mode) and, because the runner is self-hosted, achieve persistent runner compromise via lockfile postinstall scripts — an attack that hides in an auto-generated lockfile instead of the conspicuous workflow edit the old design forced. Worse for other repos: the replacement comment (L3-5) says to use 'the generic template in README.md (which adds a second checkout of frankekn/needlefish as the tool)', but no README.md exists at head (git ls-tree -r head shows only review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json), so the only in-repo description of the trusted-tool pattern is deleted with no replacement — anyone copying this workflow silently inherits PR-controlled review. Mitigating context (why P1 not P0): the unchanged job guard at L24 restricts execution to same-repo PRs whose authors already have write access, and pull_request events already use the PR's version of the workflow file, so some arbitrary-execution capability pre-existed; this change removes a documented defense-in-depth control rather than creating the capability from nothing.
