findings.title: Severity normalization removed; non-canonical severities silently demoted to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code computed `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the SEVERITIES membership check and fell back to "P1". The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` on the raw value and falls back to "P3". Because normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) feeds untyped `any` findings through this function, any severity that is not byte-exact uppercase ("p1", "P1 ", "p0", or a non-string) now rejects the membership check and silently lands on the lowest severity P3. Substitution: normalizeFinding({severity:"p1"}) → base returned "P1"; head returns "P3". A critical review finding (e.g. P0 written lowercase, or a finding missing severity, which previously defaulted to P1) is silently reclassified to the lowest priority with no error — in a review pipeline that triages output by severity this corrupts the classification signal, and existing inputs shaped like .needlefish/answers.json pass either way, so tests would not catch it. The category field's includes-style check was always like this; severity was the only field with explicit canonicalization, so this removes deliberate hardening, not redundant code.

findings.title: Severity coercion removed: "p0"/" P1 " inputs now misclassified as P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code normalized via String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase(); the new code tests raw.severity directly against SEVERITIES (["P0","P1","P2","P3"], src/shared/schema.ts:85). normalizeFinding is the exported sanitizer for untrusted review output: its only caller, normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132), maps raw: any model output through it. Substitution: input severity "p0" — old path String("p0").trim().toUpperCase() = "P0" → includes → severity "P0"; new path SEVERITIES.includes("p0") = false → fallback "P3". Same for padded values like " P1 ". A genuine P0 (data loss/security) finding is silently demoted to the lowest severity P3, and at line 132 the misclassified value is indistinguishable from a real P3 — any consumer triaging by severity buries the critical finding. The fallback change P1→P3 compounds this: even the previously-recoverable inputs now land at the least-visible severity. This is contract drift on the name 'normalizeFinding' (it no longer normalizes) and a failure-to-default downgrade on a public path.

findings.title: Drop of trim/upper normalization + P1→P3 fallback silently downgrades severities
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is fed by normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) with raw: any — untrusted model JSON where runtime severity is a free-form string despite the Partial<Finding> type. The old code canonicalized via String(...).trim().toUpperCase(), so "p1", " P0 ", "p2\n" round-tripped to valid severities, and any still-invalid value defaulted to "P1" (fail-loud). The new code uses SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) — strict equality against ["P0","P1","P2","P3"] — so every non-canonical or non-string severity (lowercase, padding, numbers) now fails the check and is silently mapped to "P3", the LOWEST severity. For a merge-gating review schema where severity drives changes_requested (P0/P1/P2) vs advisory pass (P3), critical findings that used to block the merge become silently ignorable advisories; the failure and the fallback value are indistinguishable to every consumer. This is a fail-open default on a public, exported normalization path.

findings.title: Restored GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN leak into spawned codex agent
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning 'codex exec'. This diff removes both the deletes and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its documented default env = process.env: the spawned LLM agent now inherits the host's GitHub credentials. codex exec -s read-only runs from a local opts.repoPath cwd and has no legitimate use for GitHub tokens (the read-only sandbox performs no GitHub-authenticated work), so the keys serve only as an exfiltration surface: the child can read its own environment (printenv) and echo a token into stdout/last-message output, which runCodex captures (maxBuffer 64MB) and returns to the caller. This is a review runner that itself runs authenticated against GitHub, so GITHUB_TOKEN is expected to be set in its environment. Verified against base (git show 4c6ce69:src/shared/codex.ts): the deleted lines existed solely to strip exactly these three keys; no other behavior depended on them.

findings.title: Spawned codex agent re-inherits GitHub tokens after env strip removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN before passing it to spawnSync, so the `codex exec` child process (an autonomous LLM agent running over the repo) never saw GitHub credentials. The diff deletes both the sanitize block and the `env` option; per Node semantics, spawnSync without `env` defaults to the full `process.env`, so the child now receives all three tokens verbatim. In a CI/runner context these variables are routinely set (e.g. GITHUB_TOKEN for PR operations), handing valid credentials to a third-party binary/model that can read its own environment — a direct secret-exposure regression with no compensating control anywhere in the repo (rg for GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN finds no other reference).

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrub before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `const env = { ...process.env }; delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN;` and the `env` option from the spawnSync call. Per documented Node.js semantics, spawnSync without an `env` option inherits the parent's full process.env, so the `codex exec` subprocess now receives the runner's GitHub credentials. codex is an autonomous agent that executes shell commands in the target repo; reading its own environment is a read operation permitted even in the `-s read-only` sandbox, so any instruction the agent follows (including content from the untrusted PR it is reviewing) can read the tokens. Exfiltration does not even require network egress: the agent's sanctioned output channel (--output-last-message, read at src/shared/codex.ts:33 and returned at :41) lets it emit the token as its final message, which flows into the caller's result. The deleted lines were the explicit mitigation for exactly this; nothing in the function (only prompt/repoPath/model/timeout inputs) needs GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard; untrusted fork code now runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate preventing fork PRs from triggering this workflow (trigger: `pull_request` [opened/synchronize/reopened] fires for forks too). With it gone, any fork PR causes: (1) checkout of the attacker-controlled `pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), (2) `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` executing attacker-controlled package lifecycle scripts (line 28), and (3) `tsx src/cli.ts` executing attacker-controlled TypeScript (line 34) — all on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner (line 18). This is the classic pwn-request shape GitHub documents as unsafe for self-hosted runners: attacker code executes on the runner host, can tamper with the runner agent/workspace, persist between jobs, and poison subsequent legitimate same-repo review runs that execute with `GH_TOKEN` (pull-requests: write, checks: write). The repo's own file comment ('Self-review mode: this repo IS needlefish, so the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool') confirms PR-supplied code is executed directly as the tool.

findings.title: Restoring fork-PR execution on self-hosted runner = arbitrary code execution
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control restricting this job to same-repo (write-access) branches. The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18), is triggered by `pull_request` (lines 7-9), checks out the PR head SHA (lines 20-24), and then executes PR-controlled code: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs lifecycle scripts (preinstall/prepare) defined by the PR's package.json (line 28), and `tsx src/cli.ts` executes the PR's own source directly (line 34) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` exported into its environment (lines 32-33), under an explicit `permissions` block granting `pull-requests: write`, `checks: write`, `contents: read` (lines 11-14). With the guard deleted, any user who can fork the repo can open a PR and run arbitrary attacker-chosen code on the persistent runner host — which survives between jobs, is a `zsh -l` login shell sourcing the runner user's rc files, has network/host access, and receives a GITHUB_TOKEN with write permissions via env. This is exactly the pattern GitHub's hardening guidance prohibits (self-hosted runners must never run untrusted PR code). The deletion is the entire diff, so the exposure is introduced by this PR with no compensating control.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: fork PRs now execute code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow triggers on `pull_request`, which fires for PRs from forked repositories. Base (f428391) gated the `review` job with `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`, so only same-repo PRs ran it. Deleting that guard means any fork PR now: (1) occupies the self-hosted runner, which is a persistent machine retaining state between jobs; (2) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` from the fork-controlled lockfile, executing arbitrary lifecycle (postinstall) scripts chosen by the fork author; and (3) runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR checkout with `GH_TOKEN` exported into the environment. The fork's code thus gets arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host, contrary to GitHub's guidance against pairing self-hosted runners with untrusted PR code. The removed guard was exactly the mitigation; no other restriction (permissions block only scopes the read-only fork GITHUB_TOKEN, not host access) replaces it.

findings.title: Configured duration 0 is silently replaced by defaults (was honored)
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs previously accepted parsed >= 0, and 0 is a fully valid delay for both consumers: RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS feeds setTimeout(..., RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS) at src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 (0 = SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, no grace) and RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS feeds setTimeout(..., RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS) at src/shared/runner-process.ts:123 (0 = finish immediately after SIGKILL). After this change, an operator who explicitly sets NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 gets the silent fallbacks 5000/2000 ms instead — indistinguishable from leaving the var unset, with no log or error. The base code's explicit `>= 0` shows 0 was deliberately a supported value (negatives were already rejected), so this removes a previously supported configuration silently rather than fixing invalid input.

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed: changed files outside top-6 hotspots are silently never deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block (base lines with 'tail-coverage') guaranteed every changed file lands in some hotspot ('never silently skip a changed file'). Now hotspots = sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6): if the map pass returns >6 hotspots with disjoint file sets, or omits any changed file from its hotspots, those files get no deep pass, no checked[] entry, and no residual risk — reviewLarge returns a result that looks complete while files were never reviewed. mapResult is unprompted model output (normalizeMap), so the uncovered case is real, which is exactly why the backstop existed.

findings.title: Per-hotspot try/catch removed: one failed deep pass aborts the entire large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a failing hotspot (runCodex throw, malformed JSON, normalize failure) was contained: checked[] recorded 'DEEP PASS FAILED: …', a blocks:true residual was emitted, and findings from the other (up to 5) hotspots were still delivered. Now any single hotspot failure throws out of reviewLarge, discarding all completed hotspots' findings — the caller gets a hard failure instead of a degraded-but-complete review that flags the gap. With up to 6 sequential LLM calls per review, one transient failure now zeroes out the whole run.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks discarded: candidateMerged hardcodes residual_risks: []
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code did residuals.push(...res.residual_risks) for every hotspot and fed them to the critic via candidateMerged; head hardcodes residual_risks: [] (line 113). The deep reviewers' uncertainty/blocking signals (normalizeReview produces ResidualRisk objects — the type import existed for exactly this) never reach the critic prompt ({{FINDINGS}} at line 116), so pruned.residual_risks at lines 122/128 can only contain what the critic invents from an empty list. A deep pass reporting 'could not verify X' (blocks:true) is silently converted into a clean result — failure/uncertainty and success are no longer distinguishable downstream, and deriveVerdict at line 122 receives a verdict input stripped of the blocking evidence.

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed: unmapped changed files silently get zero review
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now iterates only sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6). The deleted base code (d4afdc6 lines 98-110) pushed every changed file not covered by a selected hotspot into a 'tail-coverage' hotspot precisely so it 'never silently skip[s] a changed file'. After this change, bundle.changedFiles is consumed only by mapBundle (line 84) — any file the map pass omitted or that falls outside the 6 selected hotspots receives no deep review, no checked[] entry, and no residual risk. In large mode the critic sees only patchStat (line 117), never the patch, so these files are entirely unreviewed and the final verdict (line 122) is computed with no signal that coverage was skipped.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks hard-dropped: residual_risks: [] severs failure signal to critic/verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Trigger D (failure→default). Base collected res.residual_risks per deep pass (d4afdc6:127) into residuals and passed them via candidateMerged.residual_risks (d4afdc6:140) into the critic prompt {{FINDINGS}} (d4afdc6:143); from there they shaped pruned.residual_risks, which feeds deriveVerdict (line 122) and the returned residualRisks (line 128). Head discards res.residual_risks entirely (loop body lines 103-105) and hard-codes residual_risks: [] (line 113). Deep-review caveats — including any blocks:true uncertainty — can now never reach the critic, deriveVerdict, or the caller: a large-PR review can report a clean PASS while deep passes reported blocking concerns, and no consumer can distinguish 'deep passes clean' from 'deep-pass residuals discarded'.

findings.title: Per-hotspot try/catch removed: one malformed deep pass aborts the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped each deep pass in try/catch (d4afdc6:123-132) because runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview failures on a single hotspot were an anticipated, handled mode (the same file throws 'likely malformed output' for the map/critic passes). Head removed the handler, so the first failing hotspot of up to 6 LLM calls propagates out of reviewLarge, discarding findings already gathered from the other hotspots and failing the whole PR review. Base degraded to partial findings plus an explicit 'DEEP PASS FAILED' checked note and a blocks:true residual; the new all-or-nothing behavior converts a single transient/malformed sub-call into total loss of the review run's work.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop: large PRs silently skip unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (review.ts:98-110) pushed every changed file not covered by the <=6 selected hotspots into a 'tail-coverage' hotspot, with the explicit invariant 'never silently skip a changed file'. Head deletes that block: hotspots = sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (line 93) is now final. For any large bundle (patch > 30000 chars or > 10 files, isLarge line 30) where the LLM map pass emits >6 hotspots (slice drops the rest) or fails to assign a file, those files receive no deep review. The skip is invisible: checked (lines 97-106) only records the mapped hotspots and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded [] (line 113), so the critic and the final ReviewResult claim full coverage while entire changed files were never examined — findings on those files are lost with zero signal.

findings.title: Deep-pass failure now aborts entire large review, discarding completed passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped each deep pass in try/catch (base review.ts:123-132): a malformed/failed runCodex response was recorded as '[name] DEEP PASS FAILED' in checked plus a blocks:true residual (base line 131) and remaining hotspots still ran, yielding a partial review with explicit blockers. Head (lines 103-105) calls normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...))) unguarded, so one malformed LLM response in any of up to 6 deep passes throws out of reviewLarge and out of exported review() (line 135), discarding the map pass and all completed deep passes — the caller of review() gets a hard failure (and the cost of ~7 LLM calls is wasted) for an input the code elsewhere explicitly anticipates as routine ('likely malformed output', lines 56/63/120).

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks silently discarded; critic always sees empty list
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D. Base collected each deep pass's residual_risks (base review.ts:127 residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)) into candidateMerged, so the critic prompt contained them and could carry them into pruned.residual_risks — the value deriveVerdict (line 122) and residualRisks (line 128) consume. Head reads only res.findings and res.summary (lines 104-105); res.residual_risks is never read, and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded [] (line 113). Any residual risk a deep pass reports (e.g. insufficient evidence, partial file reads) is silently dropped before the only downstream consumer that could forward it: the critic now receives an empty residual list and cannot distinguish 'deep passes flagged concerns' from 'no concerns', so the final verdict and residualRisks are computed from an incomplete signal. This swallow is on an added/changed path of the pipeline's public result.

findings.title: reviewLarge silently drops focus/deep; {{FOCUS}} in deep.md is left unsubstituted
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, reviewLarge passed focus/deep to the map pass (mapBundle) and substituted {{FOCUS}} into every deep-pass prompt. This diff removes both, changing no prompt file. deep.md is therefore untouched and still contains {{FOCUS}} (the base code only substituted it because the placeholder exists); at head it is never replaced, so every deep-pass prompt for a large PR is sent with the literal string '{{FOCUS}}' embedded — confusing the model and polluting review output. Additionally, user-supplied bundle.focus is now silently ignored on the large-PR path while reviewSmall (lines 52-55) still JSON-embeds the whole bundle, focus and deep included, into review.md: the same user input is honored on small PRs and silently discarded on large ones, with no error or surfaced signal. Same for bundle.deep, which at head reaches no consumer in reviewLarge.

findings.title: focus hint silently ignored on large-PR path, still honored on small path
findings.whyItBreaks: At head, reviewLarge has zero references to bundle.focus (grep confirms; both hunks remove it), so a user-supplied focus hint has no effect on large reviews and nothing surfaces the drop. But src/shared/schema.ts is unchanged and base code read bundle.focus, so the Bundle type still carries focus — and reviewSmall still serializes the whole bundle into review.md at src/core/review.ts:54. Same focus input therefore produces honored behavior for PRs under isLarge() thresholds (src/core/review.ts:32-34) and silently dead behavior above them — an inconsistent, silent regression introduced by this diff with no deprecation or error.

findings.title: formatDuration emits 'Nm 60s': rounded seconds never carry into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite floors minutes from raw ms and rounds the remainder seconds independently, with no carry after rounding. For any ms with minutes ≥ 1 and ms % 60000 ≥ 59500, Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000) evaluates to 60 and the seconds field is printed as 60 instead of rolling over. Concrete case: ms = 119500 (1m 59.5s) → old code: totalSeconds = Math.round(119.5) = 120, minutes = 2, output '2m 0s'; new code: minutes = Math.floor(119500/60000) = 1, seconds = Math.round(59.5) = 60, output '1m 60s'. Same for 179500ms → '2m 60s' (was '3m 0s'), i.e. every value within 500ms of a whole-minute boundary ≥ 2 minutes total. Both call sites feed user-visible output in renderMarkdown's stats line: per-step label at render.ts:75 (s.durationMs) and the 'total' part at render.ts:80 (result.totalDurationMs), so a rendered PR review can literally contain 'p1 1m 60s · total 1m 60s'. The sub-minute branch (ms < 60000) is unaffected since ms % 60000 === ms there, making this strictly a rollover regression on the minutes>0 path.

findings.title: formatDuration emits malformed 'Xm 60s' — seconds rounding not carried into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: The new body computes minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms%60000)/1000) independently, so when the remainder rounds up to 60 the seconds are never carried into the minute. Verified: ms=119900 → '1m 60s' (and ms=119500..119999 likewise; 179900 → '2m 60s'); the old code (totalSeconds = Math.round(ms/1000), then totalSeconds%60) always produced 0–59 seconds and rendered '2m 0s'. Both call-sites feed user-visible output: per-call durations in the stats line (src/shared/render.ts:75, formatDuration(s.durationMs)) and the total (src/shared/render.ts:80, formatDuration(result.totalDurationMs)), so any call/total in the 500ms window below each minute boundary renders corrupted markdown like '1m 60s'.

findings.title: formatDuration emits '1m 60s' — seconds rounding no longer carries into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: New body computes minutes = Math.floor(ms/60000) and seconds = Math.round((ms%60000)/1000) independently. When the remainder is ≥59500ms, seconds rounds to 60 without carrying: for ms=119900 → minutes=1, seconds=round(59.9)=60 → '1m 60s' (should be '2m 0s'); ms=179500 → '2m 60s'. Base code (git show 50f8d07) rounded total seconds first (round(119.9)=120) then decomposed, so it never emitted 'm 60s'. This malformed string is posted in the rendered review footer via the calls at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80 for any total/per-call duration in [60000·n+59500, 60000·n+59999] with n≥1 (~0.83% of values per minute band, e.g. a 1m59.9s run).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 and empty string, breaking its own contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported carrier (name `parsePositiveInteger` @src/shared/runner.ts:30 and unchanged error text `requires a positive integer` @src/shared/runner.ts:33) promises a strictly positive integer (>=1). The changed guard `parsed < 0` @src/shared/runner.ts:32 accepts 0. Worse, because `Number('') === 0` and `Number('  ') === 0` in ECMAScript, empty and whitespace-only strings — which previously threw — now pass validation and return 0. Callers using this parser to validate counts, timeouts, or limits will silently receive 0 for blank input (missing env var, empty CLI flag) where the previous code failed loudly; the validation that the public name/message still promises is no longer implemented.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's name (parsePositiveInteger, line 30) and error text ('${label} requires a positive integer', line 33) promise a positive integer, but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 is now returned as a valid value. Two concrete consequences: (1) any caller trusting the public contract receives 0 where validation previously guaranteed value >= 1 (counts, timeouts, attempt limits sized off this value now degenerate); (2) empty input regresses silently — Number('') === 0, so parsePositiveInteger('', label) previously threw and now returns 0 instead of erroring, converting a loud CLI misuse into a silent default. Per Trigger C, this is a public contract carrier (exported symbol + error text) whose promised validation no longer matches the body; the promise affects the data callers receive, so no in-repo caller is required for it to be a defect.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, violating its exported positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's carrier promises a positive integer (name `parsePositiveInteger`, error text `${label} requires a positive integer` at line 33). The changed guard at line 32 (`parsed < 0`) makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", ...)` return 0 and, because `Number("") === 0` and `Number(" ") === 0`, also silently accepts empty/whitespace strings. Callers that rely on the promised validation to guarantee result >= 1 (e.g. timeoutMs/attempts/max-count semantics of RunnerOptions in this same module: a 0 timeout, zero attempts, or 0 as a divisor) now receive an out-of-contract value with no error signal. This is a public-path validation promise the body no longer implements (TRIGGER C); the untouched error message proves the accepted set, not an intentional redefinition of 'positive'.
